seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: My partner in the English Players Mr Sykes, of whom I told you, is passing through London on his way to Manchester where he is conducting a season of French and English plays. He still has hopes of a season in Paris and would like to speak with you of this and other matters. He intends to give Hamlet ou Le Distrait and has engaged as star turn the lugubrious comic Horace Rumbold to dig his own grave in the fifth act. He tells me also that one of the actors in my company made a deathbed confession that he was sent there to watch me on behalf of the secret service. He had not much opportunity, I am afraid, as my relations with the members of the company were purely formal. They were a curious collection enough but Mr Sykes made them do wonders and will again – if somebody doesn’t prevent him.

div.note: With the professional actor Claud W. Sykes (1883-1963), JJ in 1918 founded and managed a Zurich acting troupe, the English Players, which performed plays in English, ostensibly to promote British interests and values during the war (see Ellmann, JJ 423). In September 1920, JJ was trying to assist Sykes with his plan to have the Players produce a one-act play by the French statesman and author Georges Clemenceau (1841-1929), Le Voile du bonheur (The Veil of Happiness), in which a blind Chinese mandarin of the Manchu dynasty recovers his sight and becomes so unhappy with the revealed injustices of life that he longs to return to blindness, the veil of happiness (see JJ to Sykes, LIII 18, 23). The play was first produced in Paris in 1901, and an English translation was printed in June 1920 for the Beechwood Players of New York. The English Players performed the drama, under the title The Veil of Illusion, along with Alfred de Musset’s A Caprice, in Manchester, England, in October 1920 (Manchester Guardian [27 October 1920]: 1). In 1917-1918, Sykes had served as typist of some of the early episodes of Ulysses (see LI 108-09; LII 412-16; JJ to Pound, n.d. [30 November 1917], notes).

After becoming embroiled in a minor legal dispute in Zurich in 1918, JJ sought help from, among others, Sir Horace Rumbold (1869-1941), the British Minister in Berne, but without success. He came to believe that Rumbold and certain British consular officials were instigating boycotts of performances by the English Players, and he wrote a statement, dated 28 April 1919, setting forth the history of perceived outrages (LII 438-40). JJ never tired of exacting literary revenges on Rumbold, whom he cast in Ulysses as a “Master Barber” whose semi-literate letter offering his services as a hangman to the sheriff of Dublin is read out, to the contempt and ridicule of the pub drinkers, in the “Cyclops” episode (U 12.412-42). In the present letter, JJ imagines Rumbold as a tired music hall comedian whom Sykes has cast as a gravedigger (digging his own grave, not Ophelia’s) in Shakespeare’s Hamlet, retitled for the Paris season as Hamlet ou le Distrait (“Hamlet or the Absentminded One”), a phrase that Stephen Dedalus borrows from Stéphane Mallarmé (1842-1898) during his Shakespeare lecture in the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode of Ulysses (U 9.118-20). (For fuller accounts of the Zurich lawsuit and Rumbold, see JJ to Pound, 1 April 1919, notes; 8 August 1920, notes.)
The actor-spy JJ mentions is likely part of his half-humorous imaginings of maltreatment at the hands of Sir Horace Rumbold and other officials in the British consulate in Zurich.
